name: Green tea
description: Unoxidized tea — the cooling end of the tea spectrum.

tcm.note: Clears heat; the summer tea.

ayurveda.note: Astringent-bitter; light.

histamine.note: Marked by SIGHI as a DAO blocker rather than for histamine content; the catechins are the usual explanation.

stimulant.note: Caffeine with L-theanine, an amino acid nearly unique to the tea plant. The pairing is the reason green tea is described as alert rather than wired.

name: Black tea
description: Fully oxidized tea — the base of desi chai and Arab shai.

tcm.note: Oxidation warms it: hong cha is the winter tea.

unani.note: Chai is treated as garam in desi usage.

histamine.note: SIGHI marks black tea for histamine content as well as for blocking DAO — the only tea it scores above green.

stimulant.note: Fully oxidised: less theanine than green tea, and tannins that appear to slow how quickly the caffeine lands.

name: Masala chai
description: Black tea boiled with milk, ginger, and warming spices.

tcm.note: Warming tea + warming spices.

unani.note: The default garam drink of the subcontinent.

histamine.note: Tea's DAO note; spices mostly benign.

stimulant.note: Black tea boiled hard with spice and milk — a slower arrival than the same leaf steeped.

guna.note: Stimulating, which is the definition of rajasic rather than a judgement on it.

name: Coffee
description: Roasted bean brew, espresso to qahwa.

tcm.note: Bitter-warming, drying.

ayurveda.note: Rajasic stimulant.

histamine.note: SIGHI rates coffee mildly and marks no mechanism on it: the concern is that caffeine stimulates nerves and bowel, which can activate mast cells. It is not a DAO blocker.
histamine.why: SIGHI calls caffeine possibly mast-cell activating but stops short of assigning the liberator letter. Taseer assigns it, and scores a point higher to match.

nutrition.highlight: caffeine, and more of it in a light roast

stimulant.note: Caffeine and essentially nothing to soften it, which is why coffee comes on fast and leaves fast.

name: Chrysanthemum tea
description: Sweet floral infusion — TCM's go-to heat clearer.

tcm.note: Classic for 'heatiness': red eyes, sore throat.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry, but chrysanthemum's bitter-sweet character (tikta and madhura) is a reinforced case under Ayurveda's own rasa-virya rule: both tastes are independently well-established as shita in this dataset (tonic water for tikta; maple syrup and stevia for madhura), pointing the same way rather than a single unsupported guess.

unani.note: True chrysanthemum has no real entry in the Perso-Arabic canon (unlike chamomile/babunaj, a different plant that genuinely is documented there), and Unani has no equivalent of Ayurveda's clean bitter-and-sweet-are-cold rule to lean on instead — so this stays a guess rather than a grounded reading.

histamine.note: Caffeine-free; gentle.

nutrition.highlight: caffeine-free, and drunk specifically to clear heat

name: Mint tea
description: Fresh mint steeped alone (Maghrebi style adds green tea).

histamine.note: One of the safest hot drinks when reactive.

nutrition.highlight: caffeine-free unless green tea goes in too

name: Hibiscus (karkade)
description: Ruby-red tart infusion, iced in Egyptian summers.

ayurveda.note: Sour yet classed cooling — an exception like amla.

unani.note: Served as a summer cooler across the Arab world.

histamine.note: Well tolerated; sparse formal data.

name: Lemonade / shikanjvi
description: Lemon, water, sugar — the subcontinent's first response to heat.

ayurveda.note: Amla-rasa (sour) is ushna, the same rule this dataset's own lemon/lime entries apply — and this dataset's own nimbu-pani entry (same drink, different name) already reads it that way. 'Nimbu pani is a cooler' is the sensory/folk belief about a chilled glass, not the classical virya, the same distinction drawn for lemon and lime.

unani.note: Shikanjabeen descends from classical Unani sikanjabin.

histamine.note: Citrus liberator note — skip when flaring, fine for heat.

nutrition.highlight: sugar and salt together is why it rehydrates

name: Sugarcane juice
description: Fresh-pressed cane — the streetside summer glass.

tcm.note: Sugarcane clears heat and moistens in TCM.

unani.note: Ganna is textbook thanda.

histamine.note: Fresh-pressed is fine; hygiene of the press matters more.

nutrition.highlight: pressed to order, because it ferments within hours

name: Coconut water
description: The young coconut's electrolyte water.

ayurveda.note: The classic pitta emergency drink.

histamine.note: Excellent when reactive AND overheated.

ref.as: coconut, coconut shavings, coconut milk, coconut water

histamine.why: SIGHI's row lumps four different coconut product forms — shavings, milk and water alongside the meat — into one score. Coconut water is a low-protein electrolyte liquid, not the fat-rich extracted milk that's likely driving the 1; it carries negligible substrate for histamine formation.

nutrition.highlight: electrolytes in roughly the proportion you lose them

name: Lassi (sweet)
description: Churned yogurt whipped with water and sugar.

tcm.note: Yogurt whipped and drunk cold — read with this dataset's other yogurt drinks (mango lassi, salted lassi, doogh), all of which are cool in TCM regardless of what Ayurveda makes of the same glass.

ayurveda.note: Dahi/takra is ushna in the classical reading — this dataset's own mango-lassi entry says so explicitly ('a heating drink, whatever its temperature'), and salt-lassi, neer-mor and doogh all read the same yogurt base as heating despite being served cold and used to cool. Plain sweet lassi has no ingredient that would flip that; 'churning and dilution tempers dahi's heat' was asserted here but not for any of its yogurt-drink siblings, and doesn't survive the comparison.

unani.note: THE Punjabi summer cooler.

histamine.note: As yogurt.

nutrition.highlight: yogurt thinned until it can be drunk

name: Rose sharbat (Rooh Afza)
description: The crimson rose syrup of Ramadan tables and loo summers.

tcm.note: Corrected: mei gui hua (rose) is a documented classical Chinese herb, and it is warm, not cool — it moves liver qi and invigorates blood, the standard reading in TCM materia medica. This is a genuine cross-tradition split, not internal uncertainty: Ayurveda and Unani both independently and confidently read rose as cooling (gulab/ward), so TCM landing on the opposite side is a real disagreement between systems, the same kind already on record for white vinegar.

ayurveda.note: Rose is a classic pitta cooler.

unani.note: Rooh Afza was formulated BY a Unani hakim as a heat remedy.

histamine.note: Syrup base benign; check bottle additives if very sensitive.

name: Orange juice
description: The breakfast juice.

ayurveda.note: Follows orange's sour-heating read.

histamine.note: Concentrated citrus — a notable liberator serving.

nutrition.highlight: the vitamin C survives; the fibre does not

name: Cola / soda
description: Carbonated sweet caffeine.

tcm.note: A modern product with no classical entry. Corrected from 'cold' to 'cool': nothing about cola sets it apart from this dataset's other iced sweet carbonated drinks (sports-drink, tonic-water, soda-water, vimto), which all sit at 'cool' — being served iced doesn't argue for going a full degree further than they do.

ayurveda.note: A real internal tension, not a settled call: caffeine argues ushna (as it does for coffee and energy-drink), but 'sweet' argues the opposite — madhura rasa is shita by this dataset's own rule for sugar, maple syrup and the like. The previous note treated 'stimulant-sweet' as if both pointed the same way; they don't. Heating is kept because caffeine is cola's whole reason for being, not because sweetness supports it too.

unani.note: No classical entry — a modern carbonated sugar-water, structurally the same family as this dataset's soda-water, tonic-water and vimto (all cold-moist/cold-dry), which is a better anchor than an unexplained 'neutral'. Unlike water kefir or kombucha, cola isn't fermented, so the ferment-warms mechanism that lifts those doesn't apply here.

histamine.note: Caffeinated and sweet, but caffeine does not inhibit DAO — SIGHI marks no mechanism on cola.

stimulant.note: Modest caffeine and a great deal of sugar; the crash people describe is mostly the sugar.

guna.note: Stimulating, which is the definition of rajasic rather than a judgement on it.

name: Barley water (jau/talbina)
description: Strained barley infusion — a cooler in three traditions at once.

unani.note: Ma' al-sha'ir is a canonical Unani cooling prescription.

histamine.note: Very gentle — good reactive-day drink.

name: Sattu sharbat
description: Roasted gram flour whisked in water — Bihar's field-day cooler.

tcm.note: No classical entry, but this dataset's own roasted-grain-in-water drinks (barley-tea, ragi malt) both read cool, and this dataset's own Ayurveda entry for this same drink already documents, at high confidence, that dilution overrides the roasted grain's warmer lean — a reading TCM's cool verdict here is consistent with rather than contradicting.

ayurveda.note: Famous summer cooling drink despite chana's warm lean — roasting + dilution.

histamine.note: Roasted gram (chickpea) flour is SIGHI 2, mildly flagged like other legumes — gentle, but not the 0 sparse data once suggested.

nutrition.highlight: protein in a glass, from a field lunch

name: Soy milk
description: The Chinese breakfast milk.

tcm.note: Fresh dou jiang neutral-cool, moistening.

ayurveda.note: Soy is East Asian and absent from the classical Ayurvedic canon, so this isn't a textual reading — but it tracks this dataset's own TCM entry for the same drink (neutral-cool, moistening), which is the closer and better-documented tradition for a soy product.

unani.note: Outside the Unani record for the same reason as Ayurveda, but the same cross-system logic applies: this dataset's own TCM reading (neutral-cool, moistening) is the nearer anchor for an East Asian soy product than a guess with no anchor at all.

histamine.note: Soy's modest flag; fine for many.

nutrition.highlight: plant protein that behaves like dairy

name: Almond milk
description: Nut milk — modern carton or classical badam sardai.

tcm.note: Genuinely unclear rather than just 'not classical': the alias 'xing ren lu' names a real classical drink, but it's traditionally apricot kernel (xingren, documented warm), not true almond (badam) — a different plant this dataset elsewhere reads as neutral (see almonds, spices.json). Depending which the alias is meant to track, the honest answer runs from neutral to warm, not a single settled reading.

ayurveda.note: Soaked-peeled almonds ground in milk/water = the cooling sardai logic.

unani.note: Sardai is served as a cooler despite badam being garam — processing flips it.

histamine.note: As almonds, diluted.

nutrition.highlight: very little almond, in the carton version

name: Oat milk
description: Creamy grain milk of coffee shops.

tcm.note: This dataset's own oats entry (grains.json) is warm at moderate confidence; diluting a warm grain into a milk mutes rather than erases that, landing at neutral rather than a stronger claim either way.

ayurveda.note: This dataset's own oats entry is heating at moderate confidence. Unlike almond milk, there's no documented classical processing step (like sardai's soak-and-peel) that flips a grain milk's direction rather than just softening it, so oat milk tracks oats' own direction, mildly.

unani.note: This dataset's own oats entry is hot at moderate confidence; carried into a milk the same way badam's heat carries into badam milk (hot-moist), which is the better-grounded reading than an unexplained neutral.

histamine.note: Well tolerated.

nutrition.highlight: the one that behaves in coffee

name: Kombucha
description: Fermented sweet tea — trendy, and a histamine triple-hit.

tcm.note: Corrected from cool: kombucha is fermented tea, and this dataset's own pu-erh entry — tea fermented the same way — is warm at high confidence for exactly that reason. 'Cool' also sat oddly against this same entry's own Ayurveda and Unani fields, both of which already call the fermentation heating.

ayurveda.note: Sour-fermented = ushna.

unani.note: Fermented drinks lean garam — the same rule this dataset applies at moderate-or-higher confidence to beer, cider, rice wine and every other ferment in this file; there's no reason a non-alcoholic ferment should get less credit for the identical mechanism.

histamine.note: Fermented + tea + acids: among the worst drinks for histamine intolerance.

nutrition.highlight: a live culture in a bottle

name: Oolong tea
description: Half-oxidised leaf, somewhere between green and black in both colour and character.

tcm.note: Sits between green (cool) and black (warm) precisely because it is half-oxidised — the moderate everyday tea.

ayurveda.note: Corrected reasoning: 'caffeine reads as ushna' doesn't hold up against this dataset's own matcha entry, which is cooling despite an even heavier caffeine load — the leaf's tikta-kashaya character wins there. What actually moves oolong is oxidation, the same mechanism this dataset already uses (at moderate confidence) to place black tea at heating; oolong, half-oxidised, sits on the same side of that line, one step short of black tea.

unani.note: Not 'like the other teas' — green tea and matcha, also teas, are cold-dry. The real basis is oxidation: black tea (fully oxidised) is hot-dry at moderate confidence for exactly that reason, and oolong, half-oxidised, tracks the same direction.

histamine.note: Lower than black tea, higher than green — oxidation is the variable.

stimulant.note: Partly oxidised, sitting between green and black on both counts.

guna.note: Stimulating, which is the definition of rajasic rather than a judgement on it.

name: White tea
description: The youngest buds, barely processed — pale and delicate.

tcm.note: The least processed and coolest of the teas; taken in summer to clear heat.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry, but this dataset's own oxidation gradient across the tea family (green and matcha cooling, black and pu-erh heating) places minimally-processed white tea at the same end as green tea, matching this dataset's own green-tea entry at the same confidence level.

unani.note: No classical entry, but the same oxidation gradient this dataset uses across the rest of the tea family (green tea and matcha both cold-dry) places white tea, the least processed of all of them, on the same side.

histamine.note: Low; the least processed tea.

stimulant.note: Least processed of the teas, and not the lowest in caffeine despite the reputation.

name: Pu-erh tea
description: Tea deliberately aged and fermented for years — earthy and dark.

tcm.note: The ripened kind is warm and famously taken after fatty meals to move stagnation.

ayurveda.note: Fermented, so ushna — the same rule this dataset applies at moderate-or-higher confidence to every other ferment in this file, and directly consistent with this dataset's own TCM entry for the same tea, which is warm at high confidence for the identical reason.

unani.note: Garam by its ferment — consistent with this dataset's own TCM entry for the same tea (warm/high, 'famously taken after fatty meals to move stagnation'), and with the moderate-or-higher confidence this dataset gives every other fermented drink for the same mechanism.

histamine.note: Years of deliberate microbial fermentation — the highest of the teas by a distance.

stimulant.note: Fermented rather than merely oxidised. Caffeine is still there; the fermentation is what raises its histamine instead.

name: Jasmine tea
description: Green tea scented by layering it with fresh jasmine blossom.

tcm.note: Follows green tea; the jasmine adds a gentle qi-moving, mood-easing quality.

ayurveda.note: A green-tea base scented rather than reprocessed, so it tracks green tea's own moderate-confidence cooling reading directly — the same confidence level this dataset's matcha entry gets for the identical 'like green tea' logic.

unani.note: Placed with green tea, at the same moderate confidence this dataset already gives matcha for the identical 'like green tea' reasoning — there's no basis for jasmine tea to sit a level below its own near-twin.

histamine.note: Low, as green tea is.

stimulant.note: Usually a green base, so it behaves like one; the jasmine is scent, not chemistry.

guna.note: Stimulating, which is the definition of rajasic rather than a judgement on it.

name: Chamomile tea
description: Dried daisy flowers steeped for a soft, apple-scented calm.

tcm.note: German chamomile (yang ju hua, 'foreign chrysanthemum') is not the same plant as ju hua and has no entry in the ancient canon, but modern Chinese herbal-medicine sources that do treat it are fairly consistent in reading it as mildly cool/calming — a genuine reading, just not the ancient-canon 'family resemblance' the note previously claimed.

ayurveda.note: Chamomile is a European herb absent from the classical Ayurvedic canon, so this isn't a textual reading — but tikta rasa (bitter taste) is a well-established shita taste in Ayurveda, the same rule this dataset applies to tonic water and green tea, and chamomile's bitterness grounds the same call here.

unani.note: Corrected from moderate: unlike its TCM and Ayurveda readings, this one has real classical grounding — babunaj is a well-documented drug in the classical Unani/Perso-Arabic canon (it appears in Ibn Sina's Canon among others), consistently described as hot-dry, given to relax spasms and disperse wind. The reverse-of-the-Chinese-reading framing undersold how much better attested this particular reading is than its siblings in this same entry.

histamine.note: Low. It is in the ragweed family, which matters for pollen allergy rather than histamine.

name: Ginger tea
description: Fresh ginger simmered in water — the first thing made at the first sign of a chill.

tcm.note: Sheng jiang releases the exterior and warms the middle — the classic first-day-of-a-cold drink.

ayurveda.note: Ardraka is ushna and deepana, the universal digestive kindler.

unani.note: Zanjabeel is garam-khushk in a high degree.

histamine.note: Very low — one of the safest hot drinks on a reactive day.

name: Fennel tea
description: Fennel seed steeped in hot water — drunk after heavy meals, and given to babies for colic.

tcm.note: Xiao hui xiang is warm and disperses cold from the lower abdomen.

ayurveda.note: Saunf is classically shita and pitta-pacifying — the reason it is chewed after a meal.

unani.note: Thanda in desi usage, taken against acidity — the opposite of the Chinese reading.

histamine.note: Very low.

name: Jeera water
description: Cumin seed boiled in water and cooled — the everyday digestive glass.

tcm.note: Cumin is warm and moves the middle burner.

ayurveda.note: Jiraka is ushna and deepana-pachana — kindling for a dull digestion.

unani.note: Garam-khushk, carminative and drying.

histamine.note: Very low.

name: Thandai
description: Milk ground with almonds, melon seeds, fennel and pepper — the Holi cooler.

tcm.note: No classical entry for the composite drink, and the honest picture is mixed, not one-sided: several of the named spices (fennel, pepper, cardamom, and — per this dataset's own corrected reading — rose) individually read warm in TCM. 'Cool' is kept on the strength of the milk-and-seed body plus the drink's established purpose (and this dataset's own high-confidence Ayurveda/Unani readings) as a deliberately built cooler, not because the spices are cooling too.

ayurveda.note: Built deliberately from shita dravyas — milk, char magaz, saunf and rose.

unani.note: Thanda-tar by design; the name is literally 'the cooling one'.

histamine.note: Almonds and milk are low; it is the nut-heavy base that keeps it modest rather than zero.

name: Jaljeera
description: Sharp, salty, minty cumin water — sold ice-cold from street carts.

tcm.note: Mint (cool/high in this dataset) and tamarind (cool/moderate) both pull cool and outweigh cumin's warmth (warm/moderate) on their own established readings — the same balance already used to place this same drink's Ayurveda and Unani fields at cooling/moderate.

ayurveda.note: Mint and amchur make it shita overall, despite the heating jeera.

unani.note: Served as a thanda drink against summer heat and poor appetite.

histamine.note: Amchur and tamarind base — sour and concentrated.

description: Roasted green mango pulp with cumin, mint and salt — the drink given against heatstroke.

tcm.note: Tracks this dataset's own green-mango entry (fruits.json), which is itself cool/contested — 'the Chinese record covers the ripe mango only.' This isn't a separate gap; it's the same unresolved one carried through.

ayurveda.note: Unripe mango is amla-rasa and ushna in the classical reading, whatever the drink is used for.

unani.note: The standard desi drink against loo — thanda in practice, which is the whole point of it.

histamine.note: Green mango base, sour and concentrated.

ayurveda.note: Nimbu is amla-rasa and ushna — sour is heating, however cold the glass.

unani.note: Thanda in desi usage; the standard summer drink.

histamine.note: Citrus liberator.

description: Milk simmered with ground almonds, saffron and cardamom — served hot in winter.

unani.note: Garam-tar, a classical brain and strength tonic.

A high-confidence cool tea base against one modestly-dosed warm spice and two neutral ones lands closer to oolong's 'sits between' logic than to a confident flip to warm.

ayurveda.note: Saffron, cardamom and almond are all ushna.

unani.note: Garam; a winter drink of the Kashmir valley.

histamine.note: Low.

unani.note: Tamr hindi is barid in the Unani record and given specifically against bilious heat and thirst.

ayurveda.note: Ushna and tikshna — coffee and cardamom together.

unani.note: Qahwa is garam-khushk in the Arab record; the cardamom is added expressly to temper it.

guna.note: Stimulating, which is the definition of rajasic rather than a judgement on it.

ayurveda.note: Narikela is shita, guru and snigdha — cooling and heavy.

ayurveda.note: Shita and very guru; classically the wrong thing on a weak digestion.

unani.note: Thanda-tar.

histamine.note: The base is modest; chocolate and strawberry versions inherit those triggers.

name: Energy drink
description: Carbonated caffeine and sugar with added taurine and B vitamins.

tcm.note: A modern product with no classical entry, but the caffeine-is-warming logic this dataset applies confidently across coffee and the tea family isn't a stretch here — the dose is unusually high and, unlike cola, there's no meaningfully cooling ingredient (sugar is minor and secondary) pulling the other way.

ayurveda.note: Ushna and tikshna by its caffeine load — the same rule this dataset applies confidently to coffee, and here there's no competing sweet/salty rasa in the way there is for cola or sports drinks.

unani.note: Garam-khushk; outside the classical record, but all three systems converge here (TCM hot, Ayurveda heating) on the same caffeine-load reasoning this dataset applies elsewhere without hesitation.

histamine.note: The one drink SIGHI annotates with the compound: theobromine inhibits DAO. That is the mechanism people wrongly attribute to caffeine.

stimulant.note: High-dose caffeine with sugar and additives. SIGHI singles this category out for theobromine's effect on DAO.

guna.note: Stimulating, which is the definition of rajasic rather than a judgement on it.

name: Sports drink
description: Sweetened water with added salts, meant to replace what sweating takes.

tcm.note: A modern product; sweet and fluid-generating.

ayurveda.note: The previous note cited 'sugar and salt-water' as if both supported shita, but they don't: lavana rasa (salt) is a well-established ushna taste in this dataset (table salt is heating/high) — the opposite of what was claimed. The real picture is a genuine two-way pull between madhura (sugar, shita) and lavana (salt, ushna), with madhura the dominant taste by far in an actual glass of the stuff (sugar content runs an order of magnitude above sodium by weight) — which is why cooling is kept, on the strength of taste-dominance rather than a false 'both agree' claim.

unani.note: Thanda-tar; outside the classical record — a modern manufactured drink with no textual anchor in any tradition, and (per the Ayurveda note on this same entry) a genuine sugar-vs-salt tension rather than a one-sided reading, so left contested rather than forced.

histamine.note: Low; citric acid and colourings are the usual complaints, not histamine.

name: Beer
description: Malted grain fermented with yeast and bittered with hops.

tcm.note: Pi jiu is read as cold and damp-forming — unlike spirits, which are hot.

ayurveda.note: Sura is ushna, tikshna and specifically pitta-aggravating in the classical texts.

unani.note: Fermented drinks are garam in the Unani record, whatever their temperature in the glass.

histamine.note: Yeast-fermented and unfiltered — high in histamine and a liberator besides. Alcohol also blocks DAO, the enzyme that clears histamine, so it worsens everything eaten alongside it.

name: Red wine
description: Grapes fermented on their skins, often aged in oak for years.

tcm.note: Wine is warm and blood-moving in the Chinese reading.

ayurveda.note: Madya is ushna and tikshna in a high degree — among the most pitta-provoking substances named.

unani.note: Garam-khushk; well documented in the classical record, whatever the religious position on drinking it.

histamine.note: The textbook histamine trigger: skin-contact fermentation, ageing, sulphites, and alcohol blocking DAO all at once. Red is worse than white.

name: White wine
description: Grapes fermented without their skins — lighter, sharper, usually younger.

tcm.note: Read with wine generally — warm and moving.

ayurveda.note: Madya is ushna; the colour of the grape does not change that.

unani.note: Garam-khushk, as all fermented grape drinks are.

histamine.note: Lower than red, since it ferments off the skins — but still fermented, sulphited and DAO-blocking.

name: Spirits
description: Distilled rather than merely fermented — the concentrated end of the shelf.

tcm.note: Bai jiu is hot and strongly dispersing; distilled liquor is the hottest drink in the Chinese materia.

ayurveda.note: Ushna and tikshna in the highest degree of the madya group.

unani.note: Garam-khushk in an extreme degree.

histamine.note: Distilling leaves most histamine behind, so clear spirits are lower than wine or beer — but the alcohol still blocks DAO, which is the bigger problem.
histamine.why: SIGHI's row is explicitly for cloudy, unfiltered spirits ("cloudy (not colourless)") — this entry is for clear, distilled spirits, which retain far less of the mash's biogenic residue. Distillation doesn't carry histamine over (it isn't volatile), so clear spirits genuinely score lower; the DAO-blocking effect of the alcohol itself is what's kept.

name: Cider
description: Fermented apple juice — dry to sweet, still or sparkling.

tcm.note: A genuine, unresolved pull in both directions: apple juice is cool/moderate in this dataset, but fermentation usually warms in TCM (rice wine, umeshu, makgeolli are all warm). It doesn't always, though — this dataset's own beer entry reads fermented grain as cold, not warm — so 'ferment warms' isn't the clean rule elsewhere that it would need to be to settle this one confidently either way.

ayurveda.note: Madya is ushna whatever fruit it starts from.

unani.note: Garam by its ferment.

histamine.note: Fermented and usually sulphited, with the same DAO problem as any alcohol.

name: Rice wine
description: Fermented rice — drunk warm, and splashed into half of Chinese cooking.

tcm.note: Huang jiu is warm and moves qi and blood; it is used medicinally as a carrier for herbs.

ayurveda.note: Madya is ushna.

unani.note: Garam-tar by its ferment.

histamine.note: Fermented, and worth flagging because it goes into so many dishes — the cooking does not remove the histamine.

guna.note: Aged, cured or fermented — the condition the texts call tamasic, whatever the ingredient started as.

name: Matcha
description: Shade-grown green tea stone-ground to powder and whisked, leaf and all.

tcm.note: Read with green tea, which is cool and clears heat — drinking the whole leaf makes it stronger, not warmer.

ayurveda.note: Shita, though the caffeine load is considerable.

unani.note: Thanda-khushk, like green tea.

histamine.note: Low, like green tea; you are consuming the entire leaf, which concentrates everything in it.

stimulant.note: You drink the whole leaf rather than an infusion of it, so both the caffeine and the theanine arrive higher than in steeped green tea.

name: Barley tea
description: Roasted barley steeped into a caffeine-free amber brew, drunk hot or iced.

tcm.note: Follows barley, which is cool; roasting warms it slightly.

ayurveda.note: Shita and mutrala — the same cooling logic as barley water.

unani.note: Thanda-khushk; a classical Unani cooling drink.

histamine.note: Very low; no caffeine and no ferment.

name: Hot chocolate
description: Cocoa whisked into hot milk with sugar.

tcm.note: Read with chocolate, which is warm and stimulating, over a milk base.

ayurveda.note: Ushna from the cocoa; the milk is shita but does not win.

histamine.note: Cocoa is fermented before roasting, and is both high in histamine and a liberator — the milk does not offset it.
histamine.why: SIGHI's row for the prepared, milk-diluted drink carries no letter markers and a lower score, but cocoa is a fermented bean before roasting — a well-established source of biogenic amines (theobromine, phenylethylamine) — and we don't have evidence that dilution with milk removes that, so the higher, marked reading is kept.

stimulant.note: Theobromine-led, like the solid form, with sugar and milk on top.

guna.note: Aged, cured or fermented — the condition the texts call tamasic, whatever the ingredient started as.

unani.note: Outside the Unani record, with nothing else in this dataset to anchor it to.

histamine.note: Low; it is oxidised like black tea, which is why it is not a zero.
